questions.stem: Which statement best explains why fossil fuels are classed as non-renewable?
options: They are expensive to extract compared with most renewable sources
They form over millions of years, far slower than they are being used
They release carbon dioxide when burnt, which warms the atmosphere
They are found only in a few countries, so supply can be cut off
questions.explanation: A resource is non-renewable when it is replenished far more slowly than it is used, and coal, oil and gas take millions of years to form. Carbon dioxide emissions are a reason to replace fossil fuels, but they are not what makes them non-renewable.

questions.stem: Which pair of reasons best summarises the need to expand renewable energy?
options: Renewable sources never vary in output, and they produce no waste of any kind
Fossil fuels have run out in most countries, and renewable energy is always free
Renewable sources need no land, and they can be built without any raw materials
Fossil fuel reserves are finite, and burning them raises greenhouse gas levels
questions.explanation: Fossil fuels will eventually be depleted, and their combustion is the main human source of the carbon dioxide driving climate change. Renewable sources do vary in output, use land and materials, and produce some waste at the end of their life.

questions.stem: A country imports almost all of its oil. Apart from reducing emissions, how could developing local wind and solar energy help it?
options: It removes the need for any electricity transmission network at all
It guarantees a constant supply of energy at every hour of the day
It allows the country to keep burning oil without producing emissions
It improves energy security by reducing reliance on overseas supply
questions.explanation: Energy produced from local wind and sunlight cannot be cut off by supply problems overseas, which improves energy security. Wind and solar still need transmission and vary through the day, so they do not guarantee constant supply on their own.

questions.stem: Ethanol made by fermenting sugarcane is an example of which type of energy resource?
options: A biofuel
A fossil fuel
A geothermal fuel
A nuclear fuel
questions.explanation: Ethanol from sugarcane is made from recently living plant material, so it is a biofuel. Fossil fuels formed from organisms that died millions of years ago.

questions.stem: Why can a biofuel be described as close to carbon neutral when it is burnt?
options: The fuel burns at such a low temperature that no carbon dioxide forms
The carbon released was recently absorbed from the air by the growing crop
The fuel contains no carbon, so burning it releases only water vapour
The carbon dioxide it releases is stored permanently in the engine
questions.explanation: The crop took in carbon dioxide by photosynthesis as it grew, so burning the fuel returns carbon that was in the atmosphere only recently. It is only close to neutral because fuel and fertiliser used in farming and processing add extra emissions.

questions.stem: Which is the most serious limitation of producing large amounts of biofuel from food crops such as grain and sugarcane?
options: It depends on sunlight, so production stops completely at night
It competes with food production for land, water and fertiliser
It produces a fuel that cannot be used in any existing vehicle engine
It releases far more carbon dioxide than burning the same energy of coal
questions.explanation: Growing crops for fuel uses farmland, irrigation water and fertiliser that could produce food, which can raise food prices and drive land clearing. Ethanol and biodiesel can be blended with petrol and diesel for existing engines.

questions.stem: Second-generation biofuels are made from crop residues, wood waste and other inedible plant material. What is their main advantage over first-generation biofuels?
options: They use material that does not compete directly with food crops
They release no carbon dioxide at all when they are burnt in engines
They are cheaper to process because the plant material breaks down easily
They can be made without any land, water or plant growth being needed
questions.explanation: Using residues and wood waste avoids taking food or food-growing land for fuel. The tough cellulose in this material is harder and more costly to convert than sugar or starch, which has limited its use.

questions.stem: A car runs on a blend of petrol and ethanol. Why does it travel slightly fewer kilometres per litre than on petrol alone?
options: Ethanol releases more carbon dioxide per litre than petrol does
Ethanol cannot burn in a petrol engine, so it passes through unused
Ethanol absorbs heat from the engine, cooling it below working level
Ethanol releases less energy per litre than petrol when it burns
questions.explanation: Ethanol has a lower energy content per litre than petrol, so a litre of blend delivers less energy and the car travels a little less far. Ethanol does burn in the engine; that is why blends can be used.

questions.stem: What is the main limitation of solar photovoltaic panels as a source of electricity?
options: Their output depends on hot rock lying underground
Their output can be used only to heat water
Their output varies with cloud and stops at night
Their output falls sharply when the wind drops
questions.explanation: Photovoltaic panels need sunlight, so output falls under cloud and stops at night, and storage or other sources must fill the gaps. Wind and hot rock are not involved in solar electricity.

questions.stem: Sunlight reaching the ground is a diffuse energy source. What does this mean for large-scale solar farms?
options: They must be built near the coast to collect energy from sea breezes
They can be built only where there are volcanic rocks underground
They must be cooled by large volumes of river water to keep working
They need large areas of land to collect a useful amount of energy
questions.explanation: The energy in sunlight is spread thinly over a large area, so a solar farm needs many hectares of panels to produce as much power as a compact fossil fuel plant. Coastal breezes and volcanic rocks are irrelevant to solar collection.

questions.stem: A concentrated solar thermal plant uses mirrors to heat molten salt, which is stored in insulated tanks and used to raise steam. Which limitation of solar energy does this design address?
options: Electricity can be generated without needing any sunlight at all
Electricity can be generated without any losses in the steam cycle
Electricity can be generated with no land needed for the mirrors
Electricity can be generated after sunset from the stored heat
questions.explanation: Storing heat in molten salt lets the plant run its turbine into the evening, reducing the problem of solar output stopping at night. The plant still needs sunlight to heat the salt and still loses energy as waste heat in the steam cycle.

questions.stem: Typical commercial solar panels convert about one-fifth of the sunlight striking them into electricity. What happens to most of the rest of the energy?
options: It is destroyed inside the silicon of the cells
It is sent into the grid as unused electricity
It is reflected or turned into heat in the panel
It is stored in the panel cells as chemical energy
questions.explanation: Energy cannot be destroyed, so the sunlight not converted to electricity is reflected or absorbed and turned into heat, which is why panels become hot. Panels do not store chemical energy; that requires a battery.

questions.stem: Which is a limitation of wind energy?
options: Turbines produce little or no power when wind speeds are low
Turbines release large amounts of carbon dioxide while operating
Turbines must burn a fuel to start each time the wind changes
Turbines produce radioactive waste that must be stored for years
questions.explanation: Wind turbines need a minimum wind speed to generate, so output drops on calm days. They burn no fuel and produce no emissions or radioactive waste while operating.

questions.stem: Wind turbine blades are made of fibreglass and resin composites. Which waste problem does this create?
options: Old blades release toxic gases into the air while still turning
Old blades are radioactive and must be buried deep underground
Old blades dissolve in rain and contaminate nearby groundwater
Old blades are difficult to recycle and are often sent to landfill
questions.explanation: Composite blades are strong and durable, which makes them hard to break down and separate into reusable materials at the end of their life. This is an example of waste disposal constraining a renewable technology.

questions.stem: Two regions plan new electricity supply. Region A has strong, steady winds but is 600 km from the nearest city. Region B has moderate winds and is 50 km from a city. Which factor most limits the use of Region A's wind?
options: The lack of sunlight at Region A to power the wind turbines' motors
The steady winds at Region A, which would make the turbines turn too slowly
The distance from the city, which reduces the wind speed at Region A
The cost and energy losses of long transmission lines to the city
questions.explanation: Electricity sent long distances needs costly transmission lines and loses some energy as heat along the way, which can outweigh a better wind resource. The wind resource itself is unaffected by how far away the city is.

questions.stem: Where does geothermal energy ultimately come from?
options: Heat from the Sun stored in the top few metres of the soil
Heat from friction between the ocean tides and the sea floor
Heat from the burning of fossil fuels deep in the crust
Heat from Earth's interior, much of it from radioactive decay
questions.explanation: Geothermal energy is heat from Earth's interior, produced largely by decay of radioactive isotopes of uranium, thorium and potassium in rocks, with some heat left from Earth's formation. Solar warming affects only shallow ground.

questions.stem: Why do countries such as New Zealand and Iceland generate much more electricity from geothermal energy than Australia does?
options: They have thicker continental crust, which traps more heat near the surface
They have colder climates, which make geothermal power stations more efficient
They have active volcanic regions with hot water and steam near the surface
They receive more sunlight, which heats the rocks deep below their surface
questions.explanation: Volcanic activity brings very hot rock close to the surface, producing steam and hot water at shallow, cheap-to-drill depths. Australia is far from plate boundaries and lacks such shallow high-temperature resources.

questions.stem: A pilot plant in the Cooper Basin, in north-east South Australia, generated electricity in 2013 from hot granite several kilometres deep, but was not developed further. Which limitation best explains this?
options: The granite cooled to surface temperature within days of the plant opening
The heat came from the Sun, so output stopped every night and on cloudy days
The plant released more carbon dioxide than a coal-fired power station
The cost of deep drilling and of transmission from a remote site to market
questions.explanation: The technology produced electricity, but drilling to great depths and building transmission from a remote area cost more than the electricity could earn. Hot granite heated by radioactive decay does not cool in days and does not depend on sunlight.

questions.stem: Hydraulically stimulating hot, dry rock to create a geothermal reservoir has caused small earthquakes at some sites. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Geothermal energy is non-renewable because the rock is destroyed by fracturing
Small earthquakes show the reservoir has run out of heat and must be abandoned
Geothermal energy produces more greenhouse gas than any fossil fuel source
Enhanced geothermal systems carry an induced seismicity risk that needs monitoring
questions.explanation: Pumping water at high pressure to open fractures can trigger small earthquakes, so these projects monitor seismic activity and adjust pumping. The tremors are a side effect of fracturing, not a sign that the heat is gone.

questions.stem: Which renewable energy resource is not diminished, however much of it is used?
options: Groundwater pumped from an aquifer
Sunlight falling on a solar farm
Timber cut from a native forest
Hot water pumped from a reservoir
questions.explanation: Using sunlight does not reduce the amount arriving tomorrow, so solar energy is a flow that cannot be depleted by use. Forests, geothermal reservoirs and aquifers are stocks that can be run down if used faster than they are replenished.

questions.stem: A woodlot regrows 8 tonnes of timber per hectare per year. Firewood is cut from it at 12 tonnes per hectare per year. What will happen to the resource?
options: It will be diminished, because harvest exceeds regrowth
It will be sustained, because timber is a renewable resource
It will grow, because cutting stimulates faster regrowth
It will stay constant, because regrowth always matches harvest
questions.explanation: The stock falls by about 4 tonnes per hectare each year, because more is removed than grows back. A renewable resource is only sustained when it is used no faster than it is replenished.

questions.stem: Heat is drawn from a geothermal reservoir faster than it flows back in from surrounding hot rock, and the water produced slowly cools over decades. How is this resource best described?
options: Renewable in principle, but being diminished at the current rate of use
Non-renewable in principle, because the heat came from radioactive decay
Sustained, because Earth's interior will remain hot for billions of years
Exhausted, because the reservoir can never be reheated by the rock again
questions.explanation: Geothermal heat is replenished by conduction from surrounding rock, but slowly, so heavy extraction cools the reservoir and the local resource declines. If extraction slowed or paused, the reservoir would gradually reheat.

questions.stem: Which factor determines whether a renewable resource is sustained over time?
options: Whether the resource is used to produce electricity or to make fuel
Whether the resource is located on land or beneath the ocean floor
Whether the rate of use is no greater than the rate of replenishment
Whether the resource was formed by living organisms in the distant past
questions.explanation: A resource is sustained when it is used at or below its replenishment rate, and diminished when use is faster. Its origin, use and location do not decide this.

questions.stem: Which is an advantage of a coal-fired power station over a wind farm?
options: It can produce steady output whatever the weather
It produces less carbon dioxide per unit of energy
It uses a fuel that is replenished within a lifetime
It produces no solid waste that needs to be managed
questions.explanation: A coal plant can run continuously regardless of wind or sunlight, which makes its output reliable. It emits much more carbon dioxide, burns a non-renewable fuel and produces ash that must be managed.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares nuclear power with wind power?
options: Both burn a fuel while operating, but only wind power produces radioactive waste
Both depend on the weather, but only nuclear power has low operating emissions
Both use renewable fuels, but only wind power needs a mined resource to operate
Both have low operating emissions, but only nuclear produces long-lived radioactive waste
questions.explanation: Neither burns fossil fuel while running, so both have low operating emissions, but spent nuclear fuel stays radioactive for thousands of years and needs secure storage. Uranium is a mined, non-renewable fuel; wind is renewable and needs no fuel.

questions.stem: A planner compares a gas-fired plant with a solar farm plus battery. The gas plant costs less to build and can run at any time; the solar farm has no fuel costs and very low emissions. What is the best conclusion?
options: The solar farm is better in every way, because it has no fuel costs and very low emissions
Neither should be built, because each has at least one disadvantage compared with the other
Each has advantages, so the choice depends on how cost, reliability and emissions are weighed
The gas plant is better in every way, because it costs less to build and can run at any time
questions.explanation: The options trade lower building cost and reliability against fuel costs and emissions, so the decision depends on the values given to each. No single option wins on every criterion.

questions.stem: Over its life, a solar panel causes some greenhouse gas emissions even though it produces none while generating. Where do most of these emissions come from?
options: Cleaning the panels with water during their working life
Electricity flowing from the panels into the household wiring
Mining, refining and manufacturing the panel materials
Sunlight reacting with the silicon to release carbon gases
questions.explanation: Making silicon, glass and aluminium frames uses large amounts of energy, much of it from fossil fuels, so life-cycle emissions are mostly from manufacture. Silicon does not react with sunlight to release gases.

questions.stem: Which energy source produces a waste that must be isolated from the environment for thousands of years?
options: Nuclear fission
Wind turbines
Biofuel ethanol
Hydroelectricity
questions.explanation: Spent fuel from nuclear fission contains radioactive isotopes that remain hazardous for thousands of years, so it needs long-term isolation. The other sources do not produce long-lived radioactive waste.

questions.stem: Large lithium-ion batteries store electricity from solar and wind farms. Which constraint on their use relates to waste disposal?
options: Spent batteries release carbon dioxide continuously after they are switched off
Spent batteries become radioactive and must be stored deep underground
Spent batteries can be thrown into general landfill without any risk at all
Spent batteries contain metals that must be recovered or safely disposed of
questions.explanation: Batteries contain metals such as lithium, cobalt and nickel that can contaminate soil and water if dumped, and are valuable to recover. They are not radioactive and do not emit carbon dioxide once switched off.

questions.stem: Coal-fired power stations produce large amounts of fly ash. Why is the storage of this ash an environmental concern?
options: It is a fine dust that dissolves completely in rain within weeks
It can contain trace metals that leach into soil and groundwater
It is highly radioactive and gives off dangerous levels of radiation
It continues to burn in storage, releasing carbon dioxide for decades
questions.explanation: Fly ash concentrates trace elements from coal, such as arsenic and selenium, which can leach from ash dams into soil and water. It is not highly radioactive and does not keep burning.

questions.stem: Electricity is transmitted over long distances at very high voltage. Why?
options: A higher voltage allows a higher current, which carries more energy to users
A higher voltage stops electricity from being lost to the ground through towers
A higher voltage converts the electricity into a form that can be stored
A higher voltage allows a lower current, which reduces heat losses in the lines
questions.explanation: For the same power, raising the voltage lowers the current, and heat loss in a wire depends on the square of the current. Transformers then step the voltage down for homes.

questions.stem: Renewable electricity is used to make hydrogen by electrolysis, which is 70% efficient. The hydrogen later powers a fuel cell that is 50% efficient. What fraction of the original electricity is recovered?
questions.explanation: Efficiencies in series are multiplied: 0.70 x 0.50 = 0.35, so 35% is recovered. Adding the efficiencies gives the impossible 120%, and averaging them gives 60%.

questions.stem: A battery returns 90% of the energy stored in it, while making and using hydrogen returns about 35%. Why might hydrogen still be chosen for some uses?
options: It can store large amounts of energy for long periods and be transported as fuel
It returns more energy than the battery once the hydrogen is burnt in air
It produces carbon dioxide that can be used to grow crops for biofuels
It needs no energy input, because hydrogen is collected freely from the air
questions.explanation: Hydrogen can be stored in large volumes for months and shipped or piped as a fuel, which suits seasonal storage, heavy transport and industry where batteries are impractical. Its lower round-trip efficiency is the cost of that flexibility.

questions.stem: Which is a constraint on storing and transporting hydrogen as an energy source?
options: It must be kept warm or it freezes solid at room temperature
It must be compressed or cooled to a liquid, which uses energy
It is a very dense gas, so it sinks and collects in low places
It reacts with water vapour in the air and quickly disappears
questions.explanation: Hydrogen has a very low density, so to store useful amounts it must be compressed to high pressure or liquefied at about minus 253 degrees Celsius, both of which use energy. It is the lightest gas and rises rather than sinks.

questions.stem: A pumped hydro scheme returns 80% of the energy used to pump water uphill. Which statement about the lost 20% is correct?
options: It was carried away as electrical energy in the water flowing back downhill
It was transformed mainly into heat through friction in pumps, pipes and turbines
It was destroyed when the water reached the top reservoir and stopped moving
It was stored permanently in the water as extra gravitational potential energy
questions.explanation: Energy is conserved, so the losses are transformations into heat and sound through friction and electrical resistance in the pumps, pipes, turbine and generator. No energy is destroyed.

questions.stem: Three household carbon calculators give different footprints for the same family. Which explanation is most likely?
options: Carbon footprints cannot be estimated, so all calculators give random results
The family's emissions changed between each calculation made on the same day
They use different assumptions, emission factors and activities in their estimates
Two of the calculators must contain arithmetic errors, so one must be correct
questions.explanation: Calculators differ in what they include, such as flights or food, and in the emission factors they use, for example for electricity in different grids. Comparing them shows how assumptions shape results, not that one is simply correct.
